question: Why can discretizing continuous visual targets and training with cross-entropy outperform direct MSE regression, and can a pairwise feature regularizer recover classification-like feature spread without losing the target's ordinal structure?

key_findings.claim: The paper attributes part of the classification-versus-regression gap to representation geometry: cross-entropy both separates class centers and tightens samples within a class, whereas its MSE analysis supplies only a within-target tightening argument.
key_findings.evidence: The paper adopts a pairwise decomposition of cross-entropy with a tightness and diversity term, then relates squared regression error to within-bin feature-center distances under a normalized linear head, fixed projection angles, discretized labels, and a unit-covariance Gaussian reference distribution. This supports a conditional geometric intuition under those assumptions; it is not a general theorem that MSE-trained neural representations must have low marginal entropy.

key_findings.claim: The theoretical explanation depends on strong conditions that are not shown to hold or remain fixed during ordinary end-to-end training.
key_findings.evidence: Theorem 1 assumes a normalized regression vector, fixed cosines between that vector and every feature-to-center displacement, and a conditional Gaussian reference with identity covariance. The proof also needs a center whose projection equals each discretized label. Neural encoders and linear heads have scale and rotation freedoms, so loss can change projections without shrinking the full feature cloud; the manuscript does not enforce the fixed-angle or unit-covariance conditions. The final published page even retains unresolved '(??)' and '(?)' citation placeholders when calling the Gaussian assumption standard.

anchors.section: Equations 5-6 and paragraph after the proof

key_findings.claim: The proposed diversity loss is motivated by entropy but is not the entropy estimator displayed earlier in the paper.
key_findings.evidence: Equation 1 estimates entropy with log pairwise distances over samples. Equation 7 drops the logarithm and instead maximizes raw Euclidean distances between normalized feature centers; Equation 8 additionally weights those distances by label distances. Neither transformation is shown to be proportional to differential entropy. The bounded spherical geometry makes the objective well posed, but 'ordinal entropy' should be read as a distance-based representation heuristic rather than a consistent entropy estimator.

key_findings.claim: Ordinal entropy combines a global pairwise push with an optional within-target pull and adds the two terms to any task regression loss.
key_findings.evidence: After L2-normalizing features, Ld maximizes feature-center distance weighted by continuous-label distance. Lt minimizes each feature's distance to its same-target center. The full objective is the task loss plus separately weighted Ld and Lt; when every continuous target is unique, each point is its own center and Lt vanishes.

key_findings.claim: On the two synthetic operator-learning tasks, the weighted diversity term substantially lowers average MSE over ten runs, but the reported dispersion is called 'standard variance' and is not unambiguously defined.
key_findings.evidence: For the linear operator, baseline MSE is 3.0+/-0.93 times 10^-3 and Ld gives 1.6+/-0.34 times 10^-3, a 46.7% mean reduction. For the nonlinear operator, baseline is 2.5+/-2.0 times 10^-2 and Ld gives 0.5+/-0.3 times 10^-2, an 80% mean reduction. The table says mean plus or minus 'standard variance'; conventional reporting would distinguish variance from standard deviation or standard error.

key_findings.claim: Ordinal entropy improves all four reported NYU-Depth-v2 metrics on both a ResNet-50 baseline and the stronger NeW-CRFs model, with modest absolute gains on the strong model.
key_findings.evidence: NeW-CRFs changes from delta1 0.922, REL 0.095, RMS 0.334, log10 0.041 to 0.932, 0.089, 0.321, and 0.039. The claimed 12.8% delta1-error reduction is obtained only by defining error as 1-delta1: 0.078 to 0.068; delta1 itself rises by 0.010. The simpler ResNet-50 changes from 0.793/0.148/0.502/0.064 to 0.811/0.143/0.478/0.060.

key_findings.claim: The plug-in improves the reported crowd-counting and age-estimation aggregates, but effects vary by subgroup and no repeated-run uncertainty is supplied for the real-world tasks.
key_findings.evidence: On ShanghaiTech A/B, adding both terms changes MAE from 68.2/10.6 to 65.6/9.1 and RMSE-like 'MSE' from 115.0/16.0 to 105.0/14.5. On AgeDB-DIR, overall MAE changes 7.77 to 7.46 and geometric mean 5.05 to 4.72. Some age subgroups do not improve monotonically: the Many-bin MAE is 6.62 at baseline, 6.79 with Ld, and 6.73 with both, while the Few-bin GM is best with Ld alone at 9.60 versus 9.70 with both.

key_findings.claim: Feature normalization, batch sample count, and diversity weight are essential controls, and the pairwise loss can be a material training cost.
key_findings.evidence: Removing feature normalization degrades linear-operator MSE from 1.6 to 5.3 times 10^-3 and nonlinear MSE from 0.5 to 15.5 times 10^-2. The regularizer is O(M^2): on the two-layer operator model, training time rises from 155 seconds at M=0 to 1,033 seconds at M=1,000. On ResNet-50 depth estimation, M=3,526 raises one-epoch time from 1,836 to 2,344 seconds (27.7%) and memory from 12,363 to 12,405 MB (0.34%). MSE becomes worse again for very large M, so more pairwise samples are not monotonically beneficial.

key_findings.claim: The entropy curves and t-SNE plots show that the regularizer changes feature spread, but they do not validate the paper's causal information-theoretic explanation.
key_findings.evidence: The appendix reports three geometry-derived estimators and t-SNE projections on NYU-Depth-v2; Ld produces larger estimated spread than classification and Ld+Lt produces similar spread. These measurements are functions of the very pairwise distances the regularizer optimizes, and t-SNE distorts global distances. No intervention holds predictive performance fixed while varying entropy, no estimator bias analysis is given, and mutual information with a deterministic continuous representation is not directly measured.

key_findings.claim: Several manuscript-level inconsistencies narrow the strength of the conclusions even though the empirical regularizer remains testable.
key_findings.evidence: The final paper contains unresolved citation placeholders on page 5, alternates lambda_t and lambda_e in the loss description, calls the reported plus/minus quantity 'standard variance', and says an oversized diversity term causes MSE to decrease while the plotted curve rises sharply at the largest weight. These do not invalidate the tables, but they make the theoretical and hyperparameter narrative less reliable than the raw results.

method.core_idea: Regularize normalized regression features so samples far apart in continuous-label space are pushed far apart in representation space, while repeated or discretized targets are pulled toward a shared feature center.
method.mechanism: The diversity loss averages negative pairwise feature-center distances weighted by pairwise target distances. The optional tightness loss averages each feature's distance to its target center. Both are added to the existing task loss, so the method changes training only and can be attached to several backbones. The entropy derivation motivates the geometry but does not prove that the implemented raw-distance objective consistently maximizes mutual information.
assumptions: Features are L2-normalized before applying the diversity objective; the ablation shows this is essential.
Label-space Euclidean distance is meaningful and its magnitude should determine feature separation.
A batch or sampled subset contains enough representative target pairs to estimate useful global geometry.
The theorem additionally assumes a normalized linear head, fixed feature-to-head angles, target centers with appropriate projections, and unit-covariance Gaussian conditional references.
The chosen task-specific weights and target distance scale transfer only after empirical tuning.

techniques.role: Couples every sampled feature pair through a continuous-label-weighted distance objective.
Encodes target ordering and spacing directly in representation-space distances.
Bounds the pairwise push and prevents trivial feature-norm inflation.
Pulls examples with a shared or discretized target toward a common feature center.
Uses distance-based feature spread as a heuristic proxy for marginal entropy.

evaluations.setting: DeepONet-style linear integration and nonlinear stochastic-PDE operator learning with 1,000 training examples; ten runs.
evaluations.metric: Test MSE with the table's plus/minus dispersion.
evaluations.result: Ld changes linear MSE from 3.0+/-0.93 to 1.6+/-0.34 times 10^-3 and nonlinear MSE from 2.5+/-2.0 to 0.5+/-0.3 times 10^-2.
evaluations.baseline: The same two-layer, 100-hidden-unit regression model trained only with MSE.

evaluations.setting: NYU-Depth-v2 monocular depth estimation with ResNet-50 and NeW-CRFs backbones.
evaluations.metric: delta1 accuracy, REL, RMS, and log10 error.
evaluations.result: NeW-CRFs plus Ld+Lt reports 0.932, 0.089, 0.321, and 0.039; ResNet-50 plus Ld+Lt reports 0.811, 0.143, 0.478, and 0.060.

evaluations.setting: ShanghaiTech A and B crowd counting with CSRNet/ResNet-50.
evaluations.metric: MAE and the benchmark's root-mean-square error convention labeled MSE.
evaluations.result: Ld+Lt reports MAE 65.6/9.1 and MSE 105.0/14.5 on A/B.
evaluations.baseline: Regression baseline reports MAE 68.2/10.6 and MSE 115.0/16.0.

evaluations.setting: AgeDB-DIR age estimation across Many, Medium, and Few label-frequency subsets.
evaluations.metric: Overall and subset MAE and geometric mean absolute error.
evaluations.result: Ld+Lt reports overall MAE 7.46 and GM 4.72; gains are not monotonic in every frequency subset.
evaluations.baseline: The Yang et al. regression baseline reports overall MAE 7.77 and GM 5.05.

evaluations.setting: Training-cost audit for pair sample count M.
evaluations.metric: Wall-clock training seconds and peak memory.
evaluations.result: At M=3,526, one ResNet-50 depth epoch takes 2,344 seconds and 12,405 MB; operator training at M=1,000 takes 1,033 seconds and 2,205 MB.
evaluations.baseline: M=0 takes 1,836 seconds/12,363 MB for depth and 155 seconds/2,163 MB for the small operator model.

limitations: Author-stated: pairwise computation is quadratic in the sampled count M, and too many samples can worsen both MSE and variance.
Author-stated: the tightness term cannot be tested on precise synthetic targets because repeated target centers are difficult to sample.
Reviewer-identified: the information-theoretic theorem uses restrictive geometric and distributional assumptions not enforced in the experiments.
Reviewer-identified: Equations 7-8 are raw distance objectives, not the logarithmic entropy estimator in Equation 1.
Reviewer-identified: real-world tables lack repeated-run uncertainty and do not compare against later regression-aware contrastive methods.
Reviewer-identified: the O(M^2) objective and target-distance scale may be brittle for high-dimensional, noisy, periodic, or non-Euclidean targets.
Reviewer-identified: the final manuscript retains citation and notation placeholders that weaken the audit trail for its theoretical assumptions.
failure_modes: Large label distances caused by outliers can dominate the pairwise gradient and allocate much of the unit sphere to rare extremes.
Euclidean label distance can impose the wrong geometry for periodic angles, multimodal targets, or vectors whose coordinates have different units.
Small or label-skewed batches can give a poor approximation of global target order and make pairwise gradients unstable.
The diversity term can improve its own distance-based entropy proxy without improving task loss or mutual information.
When every label is unique, the tightness term vanishes; when labels are binned, center construction introduces a discretization choice.
Without normalization, the objective is solved trivially by growing feature norms, matching the severe ablation failure.
reusable_insights: Regression-aware representation learning should preserve relative target geometry rather than treating every different target as an unrelated class.
Feature normalization is a necessary module whenever an objective directly rewards larger embedding distances.
A pairwise regularizer should expose separate sampling, geometry, weighting, and center-construction interfaces so each assumption can be ablated.
Optimization of a feature-spread statistic should be evaluated against held-out calibration and error, not treated as causal evidence by itself.
Proxy or optimal-transport targets can replace raw all-pairs repulsion when O(M^2) cost or sphere crowding becomes limiting.
open_questions: Does ordinal entropy still help when compared at matched compute with Rank-N-Contrast, ConR, ACCon, PRIME, and optimal-transport tightness?
Can the information-theoretic claim be reformulated with an invariant, estimable conditional mutual-information quantity and assumptions that training enforces?
Which target metric should replace Euclidean distance for periodic, multidimensional, heteroscedastic, or noisy regression labels?
Can memory-bank, proxy, low-rank, or nearest-neighbor sampling preserve the gains with subquadratic cost?
Do improvements persist across seeds, distribution shifts, label corruption, calibration metrics, and rare-target groups?
What part of the gain comes from global repulsion, local ranking, hard-negative selection, center tightening, or simple gradient rescaling?

competitive_landscape.title: RankSim: Ranking Similarity Regularization for Deep Imbalanced Regression
competitive_landscape.difference: RankSim aligns each sample's neighbor ranking in label and feature space and was already evaluated on AgeDB-DIR. Ordinal entropy instead maximizes label-distance-weighted feature-center distances and adds a separate tightness term; its broad first-analysis novelty should therefore be narrowed to the entropy-motivated push-pull formulation.

competitive_landscape.title: Balanced MSE for Imbalanced Visual Regression
competitive_landscape.difference: Balanced MSE derives a likelihood correction for train-label imbalance and modifies prediction loss rather than representation geometry. It targets a competing explanation for weak MSE regression on AgeDB-like data: label-prior shift rather than insufficient feature entropy.

competitive_landscape.title: Rank-N-Contrast: Learning Continuous Representations for Regression
competitive_landscape.difference: RNC uses target rankings to define a contrastive objective and reports representation continuity, robustness, efficiency, data efficiency, and distribution-shift results on five datasets. It supplies a stronger later benchmark for the claim that ordered feature geometry improves regression.

competitive_landscape.title: ConR: Contrastive Regularizer for Deep Imbalanced Regression
competitive_landscape.difference: ConR penalizes disagreements between local/global continuous-label similarity and feature proximity, with special attention to minority-feature collapse and multidimensional targets. Ordinal entropy uses a simpler global weighted-distance push and does not explicitly adapt pair weights to imbalance or prediction errors.

competitive_landscape.title: Improving Deep Regression with Tightness
competitive_landscape.difference: The same research line later argues that ordinality reduces conditional entropy and proposes an optimal-transport similarity regularizer plus duplicated targets. That shift directly revisits the earlier paper's tightness story and provides a cleaner target for testing whether entropy or order preservation drives the gains.

competitive_landscape.title: PRIME: Deep Imbalanced Regression with Proxies
competitive_landscape.difference: PRIME arranges proxies uniformly while preserving target ordinality, then aligns sample features to proxies. It attacks the same sphere-allocation goal without repelling every sample pair and is therefore a direct scalability and geometry comparison for ordinal entropy.

competitive_landscape.title: ACCon: Angle-Compensated Contrastive Regularizer for Deep Regression
competitive_landscape.difference: ACCon adjusts angular contrastive geometry to improve regression and data efficiency on imbalanced data. It is a later alternative to raw Euclidean repulsion on normalized features and directly tests whether angle-aware spacing is a better ordinal inductive bias.

novelty_assessment.author_claim: The authors claim the first representation-learning explanation for why classification can outperform regression on continuous targets and introduce an ordinal entropy regularizer that combines classification-like feature diversity with regression-like order preservation.
novelty_assessment.evidence: The paper gives a conditional MSE geometry derivation on pages 3-5, defines the weighted diversity and tightness losses on pages 5-6, and reports improvements across operator learning, depth, crowd counting, and age estimation on pages 7-9.
novelty_assessment.reviewer_inference: The reusable novelty is the simple normalized, label-distance-weighted pairwise push plus optional center pull and its demonstration across several regression tasks. The information-theoretic explanation is narrower than advertised because its assumptions are not enforced and the implemented loss is not the displayed entropy estimator. RankSim and Balanced MSE already supplied competing order-geometry and label-imbalance explanations, while RNC, ConR, Tightness, PRIME, and ACCon later made the direct competitive field substantially denser.

reviewer_notes: Read all 15 pages of the exact ICLR 2023/arXiv paper, including the appendix proof, all tables, ablations, metrics, compute analysis, references, and the final mostly blank table page. Rendered every page at 110 dpi and visually checked the feature plots, equations, numerical tables, uncertainty bars, and appendix figures. The audit preserves the reported gains while separating them from the stronger causal entropy interpretation. Seven primary competitors were checked on official PMLR, CVF, NeurIPS, OpenReview, AAAI, or arXiv records current on 2026-08-23. The linked code was not executed, so reproducibility and exact plus/minus semantics remain unverified.
